claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC phase.
The approximately 1350–1100 °C interval is a critical cooling window for this alloy.
Rapid cooling through 1350–1100 °C kinetically traps local compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The trapped fluctuations are nanoscale regions enriched or depleted in specific alloying elements within the BCC matrix.
Rapid cooling limits atomic diffusion sufficiently to prevent complete compositional homogenization.
Slow cooling near equilibrium homogenizes Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 and minimizes its local compositional fluctuations.
Trapped compositional fluctuations act as preferential nucleation sites for metastable secondary phases during subsequent isothermal exposure.
The compositional microdomains lower the nucleation barrier for metastable secondary phases.
The lowered nucleation barrier enables secondary phases that are not observed in a homogenized slow-cooled sample to form and grow during aging.
Cooling and other processing conditions can affect phase stability and transformation behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Rapidly cooled samples will have statistically greater local compositional heterogeneity than slow-cooled samples.
The compositional heterogeneities in rapidly cooled samples will spatially correlate with a higher nucleated fraction of metastable secondary phases during aging.
The slow-cooled baseline will be predominantly single-phase BCC and exhibit minimal secondary-phase nucleation.
Below a critical cooling-rate threshold, sufficient homogenization occurs for the proposed kinetic-trapping mechanism to become negligible.
Extremely rapid cooling can introduce amorphization as a competing mechanism in some high-entropy alloys.
XRD and electron microscopy can characterize cooling-rate-dependent phase transformations, while the proposed study also relies on APT or EDX to resolve local composition.
